title: What the descent was for
source_text: Καὶ εἰπὼν αὐτὸν ὑφ᾿ ἡμῶν μὲν λέγεσθαι καταβεβηκέναι ὑπὸ Ἰουδαίων δὲ καταβήσεσθαι δικαιωτὴν, κατηγορεῖν αὐτόθεν οἴεται τοῦ λεγομένου ὡς αἰσχίστου καὶ οὐδὲ μακροῦ ἐλέγχου δεομένου καί φησι· τίς ὁ νοῦς τῆς τοιᾶσδε καθόδου τῷ θεῷ; οὐχ ὁρῶν ὅτι καὶ καθ᾿ ἡμᾶς ἐστι τῆς καθόδου ὁ νοῦς. προηγουμένως μὲν τὰ λεγόμενα ἐν τῷ εὐαγγελίῳ „ἀπολωλότα πρόβατα οἴκου Ἰσραὴλ“ ἐπιστρέψαι, δευτέρως δὲ τὸ διὰ τὴν ἐκείνων ἀπείθειαν ἆραι ἀπ᾿ αὐτῶν τὴν ὀνομασθεῖσαν βασιλείαν τοῦ θεοῦ καὶ δοῦναι „ἄλλοις γεωργοῖς“ παρὰ τοὺς πάλαι Ἰουδαίους Χριστιανοῖς, „τοὺς καρποὺς“ τῆς τοῦ θεοῦ βασιλείας „ἀποδώσουσι“ τῷ θεῷ „ἐν τοῖς“ ἑκάστης πράξεως οὔσης καρποῦ τῆς βασιλείας „καιροῖς.“ ἡμεῖς μὲν οὖν ἀπὸ πλειόνων ὀλίγα εἴπομεν πρὸς τὴν Κέλσου πεῦσιν εἰπόντος· τίς γὰρ ὁ νοῦς τῆς τοιᾶσδε καθόδου τῷ θεῷ; Κέλσος δὲ τὰ μήτε ὑπὸ Ἰουδαίων μήτε ὑφ᾿ ἡμῶν λεχθέντα ἂν ἑαυτῷ ἀποφαίνεται λέγων· ἢ ἵνα μάθῃ τὰ ἐν ἀνθρώποις; οὐδεὶς γὰρ ἡμῶν φησιν ὅτι, ἵνα μάθῃ τὰ ἐν ἀνθρώποις, Χριστὸς ἐπιδημεῖ τῷ βίῳ. εἶτα ὡς εἰπόντων ἄν τινων τὸ ἵνα μάθῃ τὰ ἐν ἀνθρώποις, ἑαυτῷ ἀνθυποφέρει πρὸς τοῦτο τὸ οὐ γὰρ οἶδε πάντα; εἶτα ὡς ἀποκρινουμένων ὅτι οἶδε, πάλιν ἐπαπορεῖ λέγων ὅτι ἆρα οἶδε μὲν, οὐκ ἐπανορθοῖ δὲ, οὐδ᾿ οἷόν τε αὐτῷ θείᾳ δυνάμει ἐπανορθοῦν; καὶ ταῦτα δὲ πάντα εὐήθως λέγει. ἀεὶ γὰρ ὁ θεὸς τῷ ἑαυτοῦ λόγῳ, κατὰ γενεὰς εἰς ψυχὰς ὁσίας μεταβαίνοντι καὶ φίλους θεοῦ καὶ προφήτας κατασκευάζοντι, ἐπανορθοῖ τοὺς ἀκούοντας τῶν λεγομένων· καὶ ἐν τῇ Χριστοῦ δ᾿ ἐπιδημίᾳ ἐπανορθοῖ τῷ κατὰ χριστιανισμὸν λόγῳ οὐχὶ τοὺς μὴ βουλομένους ἀλλὰ τοὺς τὸν κρείττονα βίον καὶ ἀρέσκοντα τῷ θεῷ ἑλομένους. οὐκ οἶδα δὲ καὶ ποταπὴν ἐπανόρθωσιν βουλόμενος ὁ Κέλσος γενέσθαι ἐπηπόρησε λέγων· ἆρ᾿ οὐχ οἷόν τε αὐτῷ δυνάμει θείᾳ ἐπανορθοῦν, ἐὰν μὴ φύσει τινὰ ἐπὶ τοῦτο πέμψῃ; ἆρα γὰρ ἤθελε φαντασιουμένοις τοῖς ἀνθρώποις ὑπὸ θεοῦ, ἀπειληφότος μὲν ἀθρόως τὴν κακίαν ἐμφύοντος δὲ τὴν ἀρετὴν, τὴν ἐπανόρθωσιν γενέσθαι; ἄλλος μὲν οὖν ζητήσει, εἰ ἀκόλουθον ἢ εἰ δυνατόν ἐστι τῇ φύσει τὸ τοιοῦτον· ἡμεῖς δὲ εἴποιμεν ἂν ὅτι ἔστω, καὶ δυνατὸν αὐτὸ εἶναι· ποῦ οὖν τὸ ἐφ᾿ ἡμῖν, καὶ ποῦ ἐπαινετὴ συγκατάθεσις πρὸς τὸ ἀληθὲς τὸ ἀληθὲς ἢ ἀποδεκτὴ ἀνάνευσις ἀπὸ τοῦ ψεύδους; ἀλλὰ καὶ εἰ ἅπαξ δοθείη καὶ δυνατὸν τοῦτο καὶ πρεπόντως γινόμενον, διὰ τί οὐχὶ μᾶλλον ζητήσει τις τὴν ἀρχὴν, ἀνάλογόν τι φάσκων τῷ Κέλσῳ, ὅτι οὐχ οἷόν τε ἦν τῷ θεῷ θείᾳ δυνάμει μηδ᾿ ἐπανορθώσεως δεομένους ποιῆσαι τοὺς ἀνθρώπους ἀλλ᾿ αὐτόθεν σπουδαίους καὶ τελείους, οὐδὲ τὴν ἀρχὴν ὑποστάσης τῆς κακίας; ταῦτα δ᾿ ἰδιώτας μὲν καὶ ἀσυνέτους δύναται συναρπάσαι οὐ μὴν καὶ τὸν ἐνορῶντα τῇ φύσει τῶν πραγμάτων· ὅτι ἀρετῆς μὲν ἐὰν ἀνέλῃς τὸ ἑκούσιον, ἀνεῖλες αὐτῆς καὶ τὴν οὐσίαν. ὅλης δ᾿ εἰς ταῦτα πραγματείας χρεία· περὶ ἧς οὐκ ὀλίγα ἐν τοῖς περὶ προνοίας καὶ Ἕλληνες εἰρήκασιν, οἱ μὴ εἰπόντες ἂν ἅπερ ὁ Κέλσος ἐξέθετο λέγων· οἶδε μὲν, οὐκ ἐπανορθοῖ δὲ, οὐδ᾿ οἷόν τε αὐτῷ δυνάμει θείᾳ ἐπανορθοῦν. καὶ ἡμεῖς δὲ πολλαχοῦ κατὰ τὸ δυνατὸν ἡμῖν εἰρήκαμεν περὶ τούτων, καὶ οἱ θεῖοι λόγοι τοῖς ἀκούειν δυναμένοις αὐτῶν παρέστησαν.
pass_a_gloss: And having said that he is said by us to have come down but by Jews to be going to come down as judge (δικαιωτής), he thinks to accuse (κατηγορέω) at once (αὐτόθεν) what is said as most shameful and not even needing long refutation, and he says: 'What [is] the purpose/sense (νοῦς) of such a descent (κάθοδος) for God?', not seeing that also according to us there is the purpose of the descent: primarily (προηγουμένως) to turn back (ἐπιστρέφω) the things called in the Gospel (εὐαγγέλιον) 'lost (ἀπόλλυμι, perf.) sheep (πρόβατα) of the house of Israel', and secondly (δευτέρως) because of their disobedience (ἀπείθεια) to take (αἴρω) from them the so-named kingdom (βασιλεία) of God and to give [it] 'to other farmers/tenants (γεωργοί)', beside (παρά) the Jews of old, to Christians, [who] 'will render (ἀποδίδωμι)' to God 'the fruits (καρποί)' of the kingdom of God 'in the seasons (καιροί)', each action (πρᾶξις) being a fruit of the kingdom. We then from many said few against the inquiry (πεῦσις) of Celsus, who said: 'For what [is] the purpose of such a descent for God?' But Celsus declares (ἀποφαίνομαι) for himself things that would be said neither by Jews nor by us, saying: 'Or in order that he may learn (μανθάνω) the things among men?' For none of us says that in order to learn the things among men Christ sojourns (ἐπιδημέω) in [human] life (βίος). Then, as if some would say 'in order to learn the things among men', he puts against himself the counter-objection (ἀνθυποφέρω) to this: 'For does he not know (οἶδα) all things?' Then as if [they] would answer that he knows, again he raises a difficulty (ἐπαπορέω), saying: 'Does he then know, but not set right (ἐπανορθόω), nor is it possible for him to set right by divine power (θεία δύναμις)?' And all these things he says simple-mindedly (εὐήθως). For God always, by his own Word (λόγος), passing (μεταβαίνω) generation by generation (κατὰ γενεάς) into holy (ὅσιος) souls and making (κατασκευάζω) friends (φίλοι) of God and prophets, sets right those hearing the things said; and in the coming of Christ he sets right by the word according to Christianity (χριστιανισμός) not those not willing (βούλομαι) but those having chosen (αἱρέομαι) the better life, pleasing (ἀρέσκω) to God. I do not know what sort (ποταπός) of correction (ἐπανόρθωσις) Celsus, wishing it to happen, raised the difficulty, saying: 'Is it not possible for him to set right by divine power, unless he sends (πέμπω) someone by nature (φύσει) for this?' Did he then wish the correction to happen to men being made to have impressions (φαντασιόω, pass.) by God, [God] having taken away (ἀπολαμβάνω) all at once (ἀθρόως) the vice (κακία) and implanting (ἐμφύω) the virtue (ἀρετή)? Another will seek whether such a thing is consistent (ἀκόλουθος) or possible (δυνατός) for nature (φύσις); but we would say: let it be (ἔστω), and let it be possible; where then [is] what is in our power (τὸ ἐφ᾿ ἡμῖν), and where praiseworthy (ἐπαινετός) assent (συγκατάθεσις) to the true, or acceptable (ἀποδεκτός) refusal (ἀνάνευσις) from falsehood (ψεῦδος)? But even if once it should be granted that this is both possible and fittingly (πρεπόντως) happening, why will not someone rather seek at the outset (τὴν ἀρχήν), saying something analogous to Celsus, that was it not possible for God by divine power to make men not even needing correction, but at once (αὐτόθεν) good/earnest (σπουδαῖοι) and perfect (τέλειοι), vice not even having subsisted (ὑφίσταμαι) at all? These things can carry off (συναρπάζω) private/untrained persons (ἰδιῶται) and unintelligent (ἀσύνετοι), but not the one looking into (ἐνοράω) the nature of things (πράγματα): that if you take away (ἀναιρέω) from virtue the voluntary (τὸ ἑκούσιον), you have taken away also its being (οὐσία). There is need of a whole treatise (πραγματεία) for these; about which Greeks too have said not few things in the [works] on providence (πρόνοια), who would not have said what Celsus set out, saying: 'He knows, but does not set right, nor is it possible for him to set right by divine power.' And we too have said many places according to what is possible for us about these, and the divine words (θεῖοι λόγοι) have presented (παρίστημι) [them] to those able to hear them.
pass_b_english: Having said that we claim he has come down, and the Jews that he will come down as judge, he thinks he condemns the claim on the spot as most shameful and in need of no long refutation, and he says: “What would be God’s purpose in such a descent?” He does not see that in our teaching too the descent has a purpose. In the first place, it was to turn back those whom the Gospel calls “the lost sheep of the house of Israel” (Matthew 15:24; 10:6). In the second place, because of their disobedience, it was to take from them what is called the kingdom of God (Matthew 21:43) and to give it “to other tenants,” to the Christians, as distinct from the Jews of old, who “will render” to God “the fruits” of the kingdom of God “in their seasons” (Matthew 21:41), each action being a fruit of the kingdom.

Out of many answers, then, we have given a few to Celsus’s question when he said: “What, then, would be God’s purpose in such a descent?” But Celsus puts forward for himself things that neither the Jews nor we would say, when he asks: “Or is it to learn what goes on among men?” For none of us says that Christ came into human life in order to learn what goes on among men. Then, as though some would say “to learn what goes on among men,” he raises against himself, in reply to this, the objection: “Does he not know all things?” Then, as though they would answer that he does know, he raises a further difficulty: “Does he know, then, and yet not set things right, and is he not able to set them right by divine power?”

All this he says naively. For God always sets right those who listen to what is said, by his own Word, who in every generation passes into holy souls and makes them friends of God and prophets (Wisdom of Solomon 7:27). And at the coming of Christ too he sets right, by the word of the Christian faith, not those who are unwilling, but those who have chosen the better life, the life pleasing to God.

I do not know what sort of correction Celsus wanted to take place when he raised the difficulty: “Is he not able to set things right by divine power, unless he sends someone by way of nature for this purpose?” Did he, then, want the correction to come about by impressions put into men’s minds by God, God taking away their vice all at once and planting virtue in them? Another may inquire whether such a thing is consistent with nature, or possible for it. But we would say: let it be so, and let it be possible. Where, then, is what lies in our power? And where is praiseworthy assent to the truth, or acceptable refusal of falsehood?

And even if it were once granted that this is both possible and fittingly done, why should one not rather raise the question at the very start, saying something like what Celsus says: could God not by divine power have made men who did not even need correction, but were good and perfect from the outset, with vice never having existed at all? Such arguments can carry away the untrained and the unintelligent, but not one who looks into the nature of things; for if you take away the voluntary character of virtue, you have taken away its very being as well.

These matters need a whole treatise. The Greeks too have said a good deal about them in their works On Providence, and they would not have said what Celsus set out when he said: “He knows, but does not set things right, nor is he able to set them right by divine power.” We ourselves have spoken of these questions in many places, as far as we could, and the divine words have made them plain to those who are able to hear them.

‘on our account too’ → ‘in our teaching too’ (καθ᾿ ἡμᾶς; ‘on our account’ could be misread as ‘for our sake’)
Restored γάρ: ‘None of us says’ → ‘For none of us says’
Restored πρὸς τοῦτο: ‘raises against himself, in reply to this, the objection’
Kept ‘in their seasons’: the possessive is in Matthew 21:41 and is needed in English; Origen’s text has ἐν τοῖς … καιροῖς with the genitive absolute inserted
Checked Matthew 15:24 / 10:6, 21:41, 21:43 and Wisdom of Solomon 7:27 against the verses
Crux left as the translator flagged it: φύσει in Celsus’s ‘unless he sends someone by nature’ kept literal (‘by way of nature’), no emendation adopted

Copy-text: staged source_4.json section 3 (Koetschau 4.3). Celsus’s questions are given in quotation marks where Origen reports them in direct form. ‘The lost sheep of the house of Israel’ matches both Matthew 15:24 and 10:6. The taking away of the kingdom is Matthew 21:43; ‘other tenants … will render … the fruits … in their seasons’ is Matthew 21:41 (ἄλλοις γεωργοῖς, οἵτινες ἀποδώσουσιν αὐτῷ τοὺς καρπούς ἐν τοῖς καιροῖς αὐτῶν). The clause on the Word passing into holy souls in every generation and making them friends of God and prophets follows Wisdom of Solomon 7:27, which speaks of Wisdom; Origen applies it to the Word (λόγος), so ‘Word’ is capitalised. In τῷ κατὰ χριστιανισμὸν λόγῳ, λόγος is the Christian message, so lower case (‘the word of the Christian faith’). Doubtful: φύσει in Celsus’s ‘unless he sends someone by nature (φύσει) for this’ is obscure; it may mean ‘in bodily, natural form’ (by a birth) as opposed to bare divine power; rendered ‘by way of nature’ to keep the ambiguity. φαντασιουμένοις: men given impressions or appearances by God, rendered ‘impressions put into men’s minds by God’. The staged text reads πρὸς τὸ ἀληθὲς τὸ ἀληθὲς, an evident doubling; translated once. τὴν ἀρχήν in ζητήσει τις τὴν ἀρχήν is taken adverbially (‘at the very start’); it could also mean ‘inquire about the beginning’; sense is close either way. The question introduced by ‘saying something like what Celsus says’ is a hypothetical objector modelled on Celsus, not Celsus’s words, so it has no quotation marks. σπουδαῖος rendered ‘good’ (morally excellent). ‘Works On Providence’: Greek philosophical treatises of that title; no author named in the text.
